title: Pattern Search — KMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt)
directAnswer: Find every starting index where pattern `p` occurs in text `t`. Naive sliding comparison is O(n·m) because a mismatch throws away everything you learned. KMP precomputes an LPS (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix) array for the pattern in O(m), then scans the text once in O(n) — never moving the text pointer backward. Total O(n + m).

remember.formula:
build lps[] for pattern:
    len = 0; lps[0] = 0; i = 1
    while i < m:
        if p[i] == p[len]: len++; lps[i] = len; i++
        elif len > 0: len = lps[len-1]   # fall back, DON'T i++
        else: lps[i] = 0; i++

search:
    i = 0 (text), j = 0 (pattern)
    on match: i++, j++; if j == m -> hit at i-j, j = lps[j-1]
    on mismatch: if j > 0: j = lps[j-1] else i++
rules: The text pointer `i` **never moves backward** — that single invariant is the whole O(n) guarantee.
On a mismatch you fall back to `lps[j-1]`, **not** to `0` and **not** to `j-1`. Resetting to `0` is the naive algorithm in disguise.
`lps[k]` is the length of the longest **proper** prefix of `p[0..k]` that is also a suffix — proper means it can't be the whole substring.
When building `lps`, on the fall-back branch you do **not** advance `i`. Advancing there is the #1 KMP build bug.
After a full match, set `j = lps[j-1]` to keep finding overlapping occurrences instead of resetting to 0.
whenToUse: Find all occurrences of a pattern inside a longer text
Single pattern, many queries against the same pattern (build LPS once)
You need a guaranteed O(n + m) worst case, not just average
Detecting periodicity / smallest repeating unit (lps[m-1] gives it for free)
antiSignals: Multiple patterns at once → Aho–Corasick, not one KMP per pattern
Approximate / fuzzy matching → edit-distance DP, not exact matching
Average-case is fine and hashing is simpler → Rabin–Karp rolling hash
You only need *whether* it exists once and strings are tiny → built-in indexOf is fine
remember.takeaway: KMP's one idea: when characters mismatch, the part of the pattern you already matched is itself a string whose prefix/suffix structure tells you how far you can safely jump. Precompute that structure once, then the text scan never backtracks.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand why naive matching is quadratic and can articulate the failure-function insight — that a partial match already encodes how much of the pattern is reusable.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Building the LPS array wrong: advancing the index on the fall-back branch, or confusing 'prefix that is also a suffix' with simple character repetition.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the text-pointer-never-moves-back invariant explicitly, derive the LPS recurrence out loud, and mention that lps[m-1] reveals the pattern's smallest period.

problemStatement:
Given a text string `t` of length `n` and a pattern string `p` of length `m`, return **all starting indices** `i` (0-based) such that `t[i..i+m-1] == p`.

Occurrences may overlap (e.g. pattern `aa` in text `aaaa` occurs at indices 0, 1, 2). If the pattern never appears, return an empty list.
constraints: Strings consist of printable ASCII characters
Overlapping occurrences must all be reported
An empty pattern is out of scope — assume m ≥ 1
understanding: You're locating a needle inside a haystack and reporting every position. The naive method re-checks characters it already compared after each mismatch; KMP's job is to never re-examine a text character, by remembering how much of the pattern's own prefix is reusable when a mismatch happens.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do overlapping matches count as separate occurrences?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes by default — `aa` in `aaaa` is three matches. Confirm this, because it changes whether you reset `j` to 0 or to `lps[j-1]` after a hit.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are we matching a single pattern or many?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Single. If many patterns share one text, Aho–Corasick (a multi-pattern generalization of KMP) is the right tool.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Case-sensitive and full character set?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Assume case-sensitive ASCII unless told otherwise. KMP doesn't care about alphabet size — it compares characters directly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Return indices or just a count / boolean?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Indices here. The algorithm is identical; you just collect instead of returning early.

diagrams.title: Why naive matching wastes work
diagrams.caption: On a mismatch, naive matching slides the pattern by one and re-compares from scratch. KMP uses the LPS table to skip ahead without moving the text pointer.

approaches.name: Naive — Slide and Re-Compare
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to anchor the complexity discussion — it makes the O(n + m) of KMP feel earned.
hints: Try aligning the pattern at every possible start position s from 0 to n−m. For each start, compare characters until a mismatch or a full match.
What do you throw away when a mismatch happens at offset j? All j characters you just confirmed matched — you reset to start s+1 and begin again at j=0.
Count the worst case: text 'aaaa...a' with pattern 'aaa...ab'. Almost every alignment matches m−1 characters before failing on the last.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are up to n−m+1 alignments, and each can compare up to m characters before failing → (n−m+1)·m ≈ n·m in the worst case. No extra memory beyond a couple of indices.
approaches.explanation:
Place the pattern at the first position of the text and compare character by character. The moment a character disagrees, shift the pattern one step to the right and start the comparison over from the pattern's first character.

**Why it's the obvious first attempt.** The definition of 'p occurs at index s' is literally 't[s..s+m-1] == p'. Checking that definition directly — one alignment at a time, one character at a time — needs no insight at all. It's the brute-force translation of the problem statement.

**Where the waste lives.** Suppose you've matched `j` characters of the pattern and then hit a mismatch. Naive matching discards all `j` of those confirmed matches: it bumps the start position by one and resets the pattern index to `0`, re-reading text characters it already looked at. Those re-reads are the redundant work KMP eliminates.

**The worst case that exposes it.** Take `t = "aaaaaaaaab"` and `p = "aaab"`. At nearly every alignment you match `aaa` (three characters) before the final `b` fails, then slide by one and repeat. That's about `n` alignments each doing `m` comparisons — quadratic. For `n = m = 10⁶` that's 10¹² operations, far past what runs in time.
approaches.insight: Every mismatch in the naive method throws away a confirmed partial match. That discarded prefix is not garbage — it's information about the pattern's own structure. KMP's entire contribution is refusing to throw it away.

approaches.name: KMP — LPS Failure Function (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the invariant 'the text pointer never moves backward', then explain the LPS table that makes it possible.
hints: When a mismatch happens after matching j characters, those j matched characters equal p[0..j-1]. Is there a proper prefix of that matched chunk that is also a suffix of it? If so, that prefix is already aligned with the text — you can resume from there without moving the text pointer.
Define lps[k] = length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..k] that is also a suffix. Precompute it for the whole pattern in O(m).
During the scan, on a mismatch set j = lps[j-1] (fall back within the pattern) and keep the text index i where it is. On a match advance both; on a full match record i−m and set j = lps[j-1].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building lps is O(m): the index i only increases, and each fall-back strictly decreases len, so the amortized work is linear. The search is O(n): i never decreases, and j only falls back as many times as it advanced. Total O(n + m), with O(m) space for the lps array.
approaches.explanation:
KMP runs in two phases: preprocess the pattern into an LPS array, then scan the text once.

**What LPS actually stores.** `lps[k]` is the length of the longest *proper* prefix of `p[0..k]` that is simultaneously a suffix of `p[0..k]`. 'Proper' means it isn't the whole substring. For `p = "abcaby"`, `lps = [0,0,0,1,2,0]`: at index 4 (`"abcab"`) the prefix `"ab"` is also the suffix `"ab"`, so `lps[4] = 2`.

**Why that array is exactly what a mismatch needs.** Imagine you've matched the first `j` characters of the pattern against the text and then character `p[j]` disagrees with the text. The `j` matched characters are precisely `p[0..j-1]`. You'd like to slide the pattern forward as far as possible while keeping a valid partial match. The longest run you can keep is the longest prefix of the pattern that also appears as a suffix of `p[0..j-1]` — and that number is exactly `lps[j-1]`. So you set `j = lps[j-1]` and the already-matched suffix lines up with a prefix of the pattern automatically. The text pointer doesn't move.

**Building LPS is KMP applied to the pattern against itself.** Walk the pattern with two indices: `i` (current position) and `len` (length of the current longest prefix-suffix). If `p[i] == p[len]`, extend: `len++`, `lps[i] = len`, advance `i`. If they differ and `len > 0`, fall back with `len = lps[len-1]` — and critically **do not advance `i`**, because you want to retry the new, shorter candidate at the same position. Only when `len == 0` and characters still differ do you set `lps[i] = 0` and advance `i`. Advancing `i` on the fall-back branch is the single most common bug in this build.

**The search loop.** Keep `i` over the text and `j` over the pattern. While `t[i] == p[j]`, advance both. When `j` reaches `m` you've found a match ending at `i-1`, so record start `i-m` and set `j = lps[j-1]` to continue (this is what enables overlapping matches). On a mismatch with `j > 0`, fall back `j = lps[j-1]` without moving `i`. On a mismatch with `j == 0`, advance `i`. Because `i` only ever increases, the text is scanned exactly once — that is the O(n) guarantee.
approaches.insight: The failure function turns the pattern's self-similarity into a jump table. A mismatch is not a dead end — the matched prefix is itself a string whose longest prefix-that-is-also-a-suffix tells you the largest safe shift. Bonus: `lps[m-1]` equals the length of the longest prefix-suffix of the *whole* pattern, so `m − lps[m-1]` is the pattern's smallest repeating period.

pitfalls: Advancing i on the LPS fall-back branch — corrupts the whole table.
Resetting j to 0 after a match instead of lps[j-1] — misses overlapping occurrences.
Moving the text pointer backward on a mismatch — you've reinvented the naive algorithm.
Confusing 'proper prefix that is a suffix' with 'repeated character' — they coincide only for runs of one letter.

commonMistakes: Advancing the build index on the fall-back branch instead of only doing len = lps[len-1].
Resetting the pattern pointer to 0 on a mismatch (that is naive matching, not KMP).
After a full match resetting j to 0, which silently drops overlapping occurrences.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing i on the LPS fall-back
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When p[i] != p[len] and len > 0, you must retry the shorter prefix at the SAME i. Advancing i skips a position and produces a wrong table that breaks every later search.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Falling back to 0 instead of lps[j-1]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Resetting j to 0 on a mismatch throws away the matched prefix — that is exactly the naive O(n·m) behaviour wearing a KMP costume.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dropping overlapping matches after a hit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Setting j = 0 after j == m forces the next match to start fresh, so 'aa' in 'aaaa' reports only index 0. Use lps[j-1] to keep the overlap.

followupVariations.hint: If n % (n − lps[n-1]) == 0, the prefix of length n − lps[n-1] is the smallest repeating unit.

patternNote: Prefix-Function / Failure-Function reuse. Recognise it whenever exact matching or string self-similarity is involved: KMP search, smallest period, Z-algorithm cousins, and the trie-based Aho–Corasick all spring from the same 'remember the matched prefix' idea.
